props.title: Marked Woman

sections.content: Marked Woman (1937) stands as a pivotal pre-Code crime drama that launched Bette Davis into superstardom while exposing the brutal realities of organized crime. The film's gritty portrayal of "hostesses" working in mob-controlled nightclubs pushed boundaries for its time, drawing clear parallels to Lucky Luciano's real-life prosecution. Davis's performance as Mary Dwight Strauber revolutionized female roles in crime films, showing a complex character who transforms from a reluctant mob witness into a determined crusader for justice. This influenced later noir classics like The Big Heat (1953) and Force of Evil (1948).

sections.content: Director Lloyd Bacon's unflinching approach to violence and exploitation set new standards for crime films. The scene where Davis's character is brutally beaten became infamous, with Davis herself allegedly insisting on realistic makeup to show the true horror of mob violence. This commitment to realism influenced later Warner Bros. crime pictures like White Heat (1949) and The Roaring Twenties (1939), establishing a grittier, more socially conscious gangster genre.

The film's focus on female solidarity was revolutionary for its time. The bond between the hostesses, particularly during the courtroom scenes, offered a rare portrayal of women supporting each other in the face of male violence and institutional corruption. This theme would later echo in films like Gun Crazy (1950) and The Set-Up (1949), though few matched Marked Woman's explicit criticism of systemic exploitation. sections.content: Marked Woman helped establish the template for social problem films of the 1940s and 1950s. Its blend of entertainment and exposé influenced works like Call Northside 777 (1948) and Boomerang (1947). The film's portrayal of crusading District Attorney David Graham (Humphrey Bogart) established conventions for legal drama that would influence everything from The Strange Love of Martha Ivers (1946) to modern courtroom thrillers.
